title: How to Think About Thinking - Nautilus
gist: Neuroscientist Adrian Owen used diffusion tensor imaging to study around a dozen former NFL players, finding that repeated head trauma can sever the white-matter connections between the frontal lobes and the rest of the brain, breaking executive function.

insights.claim: A retired NFL player nicknamed 'Max' began gambling compulsively, drinking heavily, and brawling after retirement, yet an MRI showed much of his brain looked normal.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Illustrates that severe behavioral dysfunction can exist without obvious structural damage on standard imaging.
insights.locator: began gambling compulsively, drinking heavily, and getting into brawls

insights.claim: In Max's case, a total communication breakdown between his frontal lobes and the rest of his brain broke a major part of his executive function, leaving him unable to control many of his thoughts.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Links disconnection of the frontal lobes directly to loss of cognitive self-control.
insights.locator: a total communication breakdown between his frontal lobes and the rest of his brain

insights.claim: British-Canadian neuroscientist Adrian Owen led a study of around a dozen NFL players using diffusion tensor imaging to examine the white-matter pathways connecting brain regions.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Highlights an imaging technique that reveals connectivity damage invisible to standard MRI, relevant to head-injury diagnosis.
insights.locator: used a technique called diffusion tensor imaging

insights.claim: The studied NFL players had sustained dozens of blows to the head and repeated concussions, with Max having cracked his skull open at least once.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Connects repeated head trauma in contact sports to measurable brain-connectivity damage.
insights.locator: sustained dozens of blows to the head
